paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: the Lord Jesus gets the whole house. Paul talks to wives, husbands, children, fathers, slaves and masters, one at a time, and every one of them has something to do and Someone to answer to (Colossians 3:18-4:1). Nobody gets skipped, and nobody gets to sit back and just watch the others. Even the masters are told, "you also have a Master in heaven" (Colossians 4:1).

So the work you do, you do for Him. Paul says, "Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for men," and then he says, "It is the Lord Christ you are serving" (Colossians 3:23-24). That changes a Monday, doesn't it? A boss who never notices you can't take away what the Lord sees, and the inheritance comes from Him. And since "there is no favoritism" (Colossians 3:25), the same standard sits over everybody, and the same Lord watches over everybody.

Then Paul brings it all into prayer and everyday words. "Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful," he says, and he asks for prayer for himself, in chains, that God would open a door for the word (Colossians 4:2-3). I think that tells you where he puts his hope. Chains can't lock up the message. Live wisely with outsiders, "redeeming the time," and let your speech be "gracious, seasoned with salt" (Colossians 4:5-6). That's a baker whose whole day, from the kitchen table to the conversation at the door, belongs to Jesus.
